narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1st) after your first year and only slightly higher (2nd decile) by your third year. In contrast, students who were accepted typically ranked around the 6th decile in both periods. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the third most important factor. This score worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, its positive influence was not large enough to overcome the negative effect of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30, family income bracket, and plan to attend full-time were considered but had far less impact on the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
